name: Low-sodium diet / salt reduction
lead: A low-sodium diet limits dietary salt. In medicine it is used mainly to lower blood pressure. In looksmaxxing communities, salt reduction is discussed as a way to reduce water retention and morning facial puffiness, and it is also contested within those communities.

Trials show that lowering sodium reduces blood pressure, and health agencies advise lower salt intake.[1][4] A general reference on puffy eyes lists excess sodium as a possible contributor to fluid retention, though it marks the claim as needing a citation.[5] No trial has tested sodium restriction against facial puffiness.

paras: In the DASH-Sodium trial, 412 participants ate either a typical US control diet or the DASH diet at different sodium levels, and lower sodium reduced blood pressure in people with and without hypertension.[1] The Intersalt study of 10,079 adults in 52 centres examined the relation between 24-hour urinary sodium and potassium and blood pressure.[2]

The American Heart Association, CDC, EFSA and WHO advise reducing salt intake. A 2016 review found evidence on cardiovascular events and deaths mixed, and some researchers question benefits for whole populations. Sodium sensitivity has no universally accepted definition, and about 15% of adults show inverse sensitivity.[4][3]

Water retention is the mechanism by which salt raises blood pressure.[4] Sources describing puffy eyes name excess sodium, pregnancy and menstrual hormones among causes of fluid retention under the eyes, and the sodium claim is flagged as needing a citation.[5]

Some forum users argue the opposite of the usual advice: that chronically low sodium raises aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone, increasing retention, and that higher sodium with high water intake reduces bloat; they cite bodybuilding practice.[6] Other users avoid salt before photos or events. These positions are asserted in forum posts, and no study cited here has tested either for facial appearance.

No studies found on sodium reduction and facial puffiness or appearance. Blood pressure trials such as DASH-Sodium and observational data such as Intersalt are the main human research on dietary sodium.[1][2]

timeline.event: Intersalt publishes 24-hour urinary electrolyte and blood pressure data from 52 centres.[2]
DASH-Sodium trial reports effects of sodium levels on blood pressure.[1]

lore.intro: Sodium is discussed both as a cause of bloat and, by some, as something whose restriction backfires.

claims.claim: Cutting salt reduces facial bloat and morning puffiness
claims.believers: Proponents say sodium causes water retention and that lowering intake leaves the face leaner and less swollen.
claims.experts: Trials show lower sodium reduces blood pressure; a general reference lists sodium as a possible contributor to puffy eyes with a citation still needed. No facial-appearance trial exists.[1][5]

claims.claim: Very low sodium worsens water retention via aldosterone
claims.believers: A forum thread argues that low intake raises aldosterone and ADH, so people should eat more sodium and drink more water to reduce bloat.[6]
claims.experts: Reviews note sodium sensitivity has no accepted definition and responses vary between people; no study cited here tests this claim for appearance.[3][4]

card.summary: Salt cutting for less bloat; proven for blood pressure, untested for faces, and argued both ways online.
card.note: Evidence is for blood pressure, not appearance; sodium needs vary and people with medical conditions follow clinician advice.

quick.overview:
Low-sodium eating is a standard blood pressure measure. Appearance communities use it to try to reduce water retention and facial puffiness.

Some forum users argue the reverse, that very low sodium increases retention. Neither view has been tested for how the face looks.
quick.mechanism: Sodium influences how much water the body holds; less sodium is expected to mean less retained fluid.
quick.risks: Guidelines advise lower salt for most adults, but reviews note mixed evidence on outcomes and some people respond inversely. Medical conditions may call for clinician guidance.
